sec:introduction-overview:
The starting point is a collection of observations about how an observer interacts with the world. Colours are seen, and three of them mix to produce white. An observer moves around, rotates, and looks from different angles, yet the things measured do not depend on where the observer stands or which way it faces. Time flows in one direction, and observers are carried along with it. Three-fold structure recurs throughout nature — three colours, three generations of matter, three-fold chirality — too insistently to be coincidence; it asks for explanation rather than stipulation. Multiple observers share the same world; they do not each illuminate a private universe but navigate a common landscape.

Some observations run deeper. Observers measure, record, and compare, and the comparisons are consistent: there is a pairing between what is observed and the instruments used. Smooth change is the rule across scales, so linear approximation describes the world from planetary orbits to particle scattering, with integration and differentiation as its native operations. Things occupy space, and that space can be measured — the universe has volume. There is the experience of choice: an observer decides what to measure and when, and the decision shapes what is recorded. Whether that experience reflects something in the structure of the world, or only ignorance of it, is a question rather than a premise; the paper returns to it when observation is treated as a process inside the structure (Measurement and Observation). Even the capacity for computation — to reason, count, and calculate — seems woven into the fabric rather than added on.

One assumption is deliberately left out: that the constants of nature are constant. A physical theory usually takes its constants as fixed numbers, measured once and then held still. If they are allowed to vary — not arbitrarily, but in a controlled, algebraic way — how does that change the mechanics, or more precisely the mechanics of observation? That is the question the paper asks, and the aether parameter below is the form it takes.

Einstein taught that geometry and mass are bound together: spacetime is not a passive stage on which matter performs, but a participant shaped by the matter it contains. The motivating hope here is that a similar bond holds one level down, between the algebra of processes and the mass and interactions of what those processes describe. The algebraic counterpart of curvature is torsion — the failure of two operations to commute — and the paper asks how much of the structure of particles that failure can carry. Gravity itself is taken up in its own chapter (Gravity and Spacetime Emergence).

Heisenberg wrote that "what we observe is not nature in itself but nature exposed to our method of questioning" [heisenberg1958]. So the question is not what the universe is but what its mechanics do — how its processes compose and transform. Wigner found the effectiveness of mathematics in describing nature "unreasonable", a "wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve" [wigner1960]. The approach of this paper is to take that unreasonableness not as a mystery to be explained but as a principle to be axiomatised: the paper posits that the observable universe is the mathematical structure its own observations force, so that the fit between mathematics and the world is built in rather than discovered.

The natural home for such a structure is category theory, the study of how processes combine. A category records objects and the processes (morphisms) between them, and says how processes compose; a monoidal category also says how two processes run side by side. The language describes structure and transformation without committing to any picture of what the underlying objects "really are". The guiding example is familiar from a first course on Lie groups: the finite-dimensional representations of \mathrm{SU}(2), with their tensor products, duals, and the forgetful map that remembers only the underlying vector space. From that data alone the Tannaka–Krein theorem reconstructs the group itself (Tannaka–Krein reconstruction); the symmetry is recovered from how its representations compose rather than assumed in advance.

The central thesis is that the everyday observations above, once stated carefully, single out one kind of structure: a category of processes rich enough to integrate, to differentiate, and to be measured against. Each observation becomes one ingredient. Duality — every process has a reverse — is the rigidity of the category. Consistent measurement is a fibre functor \tau, which sends each object to the vector space an instrument reads. Integration is a trace: on the \mathrm{SU}(2) example it is exactly the Haar integral over the group (Frobenius pairing on \mathrm{SU}(2)). Volume is the requirement that this trace be non-degenerate. A structure that meets all of these requirements, including that its states be observable and its measurements consistent, is called a quantum observable universe (QOU) (definition). The force of the thesis is that the observations determine the ingredients; nothing else is added by hand.

This starting point is relational in the sense Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz set out in his 1715--1716 correspondence with Samuel Clarke [leibniz-clarke1717, earman1989]: sequential composition (\circ) records the chronological order of successions, the monoidal product and braiding (\otimes, \sigma) record the order of coexistences, and the Principle of the Identity of Indiscernibles equates processes that agree on every closed trace pairing. On the n-strand Iwahori--Hecke braid algebra H_n(q) equipped with the Jones--Markov trace \tau_q at parameter z = q^3/(q^2 + 1), the trace radical \mathrm{rad}\,\tau_q = \{a \in H_n(q) : \tau_q(a b) = 0 \text{ for all } b\} vanishes for n \le 2 and is nonzero for every n \ge 3, where three-strand antisymmetrisation annihilates all trace pairings and blocks any finite spectral distance on H_n(q) (Gram degeneracy). Quotienting by that null ideal in the algebraic sense of Israel M. Gelfand, Mark A. Naimark, and Irving E. Segal [gelfand-naimark1943, segal1947] yields, for nonzero q \in \mathbb{C} with q^k \neq 1 (k \ge 1), the planar Temperley--Lieb algebra H_n(q)/\mathrm{rad}\,\tau_q \cong TL_n(q + q^{-1}) (Temperley--Lieb trace-radical quotient), on whose faithful state space Marc A. Rieffel's compact quantum metric seminorms [rieffel1999] induce a finite Kantorovich--Rubinstein transport metric (Rieffel quotient faithfulness). Unlike the classical relational mechanics of Julian B. Barbour and Bruno Bertotti [barbour-bertotti1982], which quotients a pre-existing Euclidean configuration space \mathbb{R}^{3N} by rigid motions, and unlike Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics [rovelli1996], which indexes Hilbert-space state vectors to pairs of observers while leaving the spacetime metric external, a quantum observable universe posits no spatial manifold at the outset and enforces inter-observer consistency through the shared fibre functor \tau. Downstream, this relational chain yields strictly pseudoconvex contact Cauchy--Riemann three-manifolds whose canonical circle bundle carries Charles L. Fefferman's kinematic (3, 1) Lorentzian metric, while dynamical Einstein field equations on that four-manifold remain conjectural (Lorentzian circle-bundle lift, Gravity and Spacetime Emergence).

The categorical language then recovers, as internal pieces of the structure, the concepts that describe a universe's mechanics. The Lagrangian is a trace and the action is an integral (categorical action); curvature, the gauge field, and the matter current are specific processes in the category; the Dirac operator is a connection twisted by the system's own internal time-flow (categorical Dirac operator). Each is a construction the axioms allow, not an entry borrowed from the classical dictionary.

Noether taught that every continuous symmetry of a physical system yields a conserved quantity: invariance under rotation gives angular momentum, under translation in time gives energy, under a change of gauge gives charge. Her theorem is the bridge from the symmetries that are observed to the quantities that are measured, and it suggests why a trace should be the notion of integration here: a trace is a device for extracting one number from a symmetric process. Once the structure is deformed by the parameter of the next section, the bridge bends rather than breaks: the conserved quantities acquire corrections, and some identities that held exactly become approximate ones (Noether's theorem in the q-deformed setting).
prose:intro-aether-parameter:
The structure does not come alone; it comes as a family. The everyday operations of calculus have a deformation: the full derivative and its projection onto the internal time-flow combine into a one-parameter family of first-order operators,

  d_q = q^{-1} d + (1 - q^{-1})\,\pi_V \circ d,

and the parameter q that labels the family is the aether parameter (definition). On \mathrm{SU}(2), with left-invariant forms \omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3 and the Hopf fibre S^1 \to S^3 \to S^2 generated by the vector field \xi dual to \omega_3, the projection \pi_V keeps only the fibre component: \pi_V(df) = \xi(f)\,\omega_3 (Reeb vector on \mathrm{SU}(2)). At q = 1 the operator d_q is the ordinary derivative and the classical calculus returns. Away from q = 1 every construction in the paper acquires a q-dependence, and a single small quantity,

  \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1},

measures how far a given member of the family sits from the classical one. The same quantity reappears as the size of the commutator of position and momentum: the uncertainty relation is the measurement of a displacement along the internal time-flow, which vanishes at q = 1 (Heisenberg commutator).

This changes the shape of the question the paper asks. The constants of a physical theory are usually taken as given. Here the categorical computations are carried out for every q at once — the traces they produce are rational functions of q with rational coefficients (derivation chain) — and only at the very end is a particular value q_0 substituted. The observed universe is then one member of a family of mathematically consistent universes, picked out by measurement rather than by the axioms. Which member, and how it is picked out, is the subject of the calibration discussed below.
prose:intro-particles-as-knots:
The state space on which all of this lives is not free to take any shape. It is a compact Riemann surface, and its Euler characteristic \chi = 2 - 2g records its genus g. The lifting obstructions of the foundational chapters force g \geq 1; the Descartes condition \chi = -6 fixes g = 4. Among the universes satisfying that condition one surface is terminal: Bring's curve of genus four, whose automorphism group is the symmetric group S_5 (Descartes theorem; Bring's surface).

Particles are modelled as knots and links in this setting. The dictionary is a naming convention for constructions inside the model, in the way a topologist calls a particular knot "the trefoil": a loop with no crossings is the lightest, most elusive particle, the neutrino; a single over–under knot, the trefoil, is the electron; two loops linked once, the Hopf link, is the strong binding of quarks; three loops linked so that no two are directly joined, the Borromean rings, is the proton or neutron. The same objects can be read as vortex lines in a fluid, and the later chapters use both pictures.

The idea that particles are knots has a history. Helmholtz proved in 1858 that in an ideal fluid a vortex tube moves with the flow and keeps its strength [helmholtz1858], so a knotted vortex ring keeps its knot type. In 1867 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed that atoms are knotted and linked vortex rings in the ether, one knot type for each element [thomson1867vortexatoms]. Maxwell took the idea seriously and recorded Gauss's integral for the linking number of two closed curves [maxwell1873treatise2], and Tait's tables of knots, begun to give the vortex atoms a periodic table, started knot theory as a subject [tait1877knots]. The vortex atom was abandoned by about 1900 [kragh2002vortexatom], but knotted particles have returned: as knotted solitons in field theory in the work of Ludvig Faddeev and Antti J. Niemi [faddeevniemi1997], in the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) quantum-knot representation model of Robert J. Finkelstein [finkelstein2007, finkelstein2008], in the three-strand braided-ribbon preon models of Sundance Bilson-Thompson [bilson-thompson2005], of Sundance Bilson-Thompson, Fotini Markopoulou, and Lee Smolin [bilsonthompson2007], and of Sundance Bilson-Thompson, Jonathan Hackett, and Louis H. Kauffman [bilson-thompson-hackett-kauffman2009], and in Joel Avrin's band model, where the unknot and the trefoil bound the surfaces that model the elementary fermions [avrin-2012]. This paper keeps the combinatorics of that lineage — knot and braid types and the algebra of their crossings — rather than the ether or ribbon-twist preon assignments; the chapter on knots and particles gives a fuller account (Knots, Particles, and Confinement).

Two later programmes share the categorical setting without the knots. In algebraic quantum field theory in four spacetime dimensions, Sergio Doplicher, Rudolf Haag, and John E. Roberts showed that the local superselection sectors form a symmetric tensor category in which the braid group factors through the symmetric group [doplicher-haag-roberts1971], and Sergio Doplicher and John E. Roberts reconstructed a compact gauge group from that category [doplicher-roberts1989]; braided sector statistics arise in two and three spacetime dimensions in the frameworks of Klaus Fredenhagen, Karl-Henning Rehren, and Bert Schroer [fredenhagen-rehren-schroer1989] and of Jürg Fröhlich and Fabrizio Gabbiani [frohlich-gabbiani1990]. In categorical quantum mechanics, Samson Abramsky and Bob Coecke [abramsky-coecke2004] and Peter Selinger [selinger2007] formulated finite-dimensional quantum processes inside \dagger-compact closed categories, within which Bob Coecke, Dusko Pavlovic, and Jamie Vicary proved that commutative special \dagger-Frobenius algebras correspond to orthonormal bases [coecke-pavlovic-vicary2013]. Both programmes take particle masses as external parameters. This paper differs in working inside a braided category with \sigma_i^2 \neq 1 and testing whether dimensionless invariants can be read off closed braids through a Markov trace. Four scope boundaries fix what is and is not claimed: every Frobenius object used in the construction has finite rank; the proton-to-electron ratio m_{\mathfrak{p}}/m_e serves as the numerical pin that fixes the evaluation point q_0, not as a derived output (the ideal calibration proxy for the same modulus is m_\mu/m_e; which pin the numbers use); the overall magnitude of nuclear binding energies is open; and a derivation of the fermion generation count from Bring's curve is not established. How far the derived ratios agree with experiment within those boundaries is the subject of the comparison chapters.

The algebra that describes how such strands cross is the Iwahori–Hecke algebra H_n(q). Its generator \sigma_i crosses strand i over strand i+1, and the only rule beyond the braid relations is one quadratic equation,

  (\sigma_i - q)(\sigma_i + q^{-1}) = 0,

which says that a crossing has exactly two eigenvalues, q and -q^{-1}. At q = 1 the equation reads \sigma_i^2 = 1 and the algebra is the group algebra \mathbb{C}[S_n] of the symmetric group, which a first course in representation theory splits into matrix blocks, one for each irreducible representation. For n = 3 the splitting is \mathbb{C}[S_3] \cong \mathbb{C} \oplus \mathbb{C} \oplus M_2(\mathbb{C}), of total dimension six; the deformation keeps this shape.

The photon stands apart. It is not a knot but a blend of the four simplest operations,

  \gamma = 1 + \varphi_0\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\,\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1},

the identity together with the elementary crossings \sigma_0, \sigma_1 and the pair-production vertex \sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1}. This is what lets light build matter: when two photons meet, their terms multiply out under the quadratic relation and reach every operator of a six-element basis of H_3(q) (pair production). The embeddability bound on the genus-four surface keeps the operator content at exactly that six-dimensional algebra, so the list of elementary interactions is finite.

One object recurs at the framework's hardest edges: an obstruction class, the precise measure of when local data fails to extend globally (lifting condition). In the q-deformed settings of the later chapters, questions about the smoothness of a fluid, about shortcuts in a computation and about the zeros of a zeta function are each translated into a question about a class of this kind. The translations are where the open content lies, and sharing a class does not by itself make the answers agree.
prose:intro-structure-to-numbers:
The route from the axioms to a number that can be compared with experiment passes through a short sequence of steps, each of them a standard construction applied to the structure above. They are stated here in words; the mass-analysis chapter records each step with its algorithm (derivation chain).

  1. From processes to braids. A configuration of strands followed through the internal time-flow traces out a braid, and composing processes composes braids. The braiding of the category therefore gives a representation of the braid group, and integrating it over surfaces lands in the Iwahori–Hecke algebra H_n(q).

  2. From braids to knots. Joining the ends of a braid closes it into a knot or link. A theorem of Jones and Ocneanu gives a unique normalised trace on H_n(q) compatible with closing, the Markov trace \mathrm{tr}_M, and evaluated on a closed braid it is the Jones polynomial J_K(q) (Markov trace). Each knot thus receives a rational function of q.

  3. From one trace to finitely many pieces. The algebra H_n(q) splits into matrix blocks indexed by the partitions \lambda of n, exactly as \mathbb{C}[S_n] does at q = 1. On each block the trace is an ordinary matrix trace, the character \chi_\lambda, so the Markov trace becomes a finite weighted sum \mathrm{tr}_M = \sum_\lambda y_\lambda \chi_\lambda — the Fourier decomposition of the trace over the irreducible blocks (Wedderburn decomposition).

  4. From many candidates to one element. Which element of the algebra represents a given composite is not chosen by hand. Candidates are built by pair production from photons, and a semidefinite program over the Frobenius pairing selects among them; its dual variables record which blocks the selected state saturates (confinement program). Where this selection is complete and where it is still open is recorded composite by composite in the nuclear and mass chapters.

  5. From rational functions to numbers. Everything up to this point is algebra in the variable q. The last step is the archimedean realisation: substitute the measured value q_0 and multiply by a single unit of scale (archimedean functor).

A worked miniature. Write h = q - q^{-1}, so that the quadratic relation reads \sigma_i^2 = h\sigma_i + 1 and \sigma_i^{-1} = \sigma_i - h, and let z = q^3/(q^2+1) be the Markov parameter. Take the three-strand word V^3 = (\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1})^3, the core of the Borromean rings, and follow it along the route above.

  1. Braid to algebra. Replacing each \sigma_1^{-1} by \sigma_1 - h and reducing with \sigma_i^2 = h\sigma_i + 1 leaves a combination of the six basis elements 1, \sigma_0, \sigma_1, \sigma_0\sigma_1, \sigma_1\sigma_0, \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 of H_3(q) with coefficients in \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}].
  2. Trace. The Markov trace sends these six elements to 1, z, z, z^2, z^2, z(hz+1), and the sum collapses to \mathrm{tr}_M(V^3) = \frac{4 + h^2 - 3h^4 - h^6}{h^2 + 4}.
  3. Blocks. The same rational function is \sum_\lambda y_\lambda\chi_\lambda over \lambda = (3), (2,1), (1^3), with y_{(3)} = \frac{q^4+1}{(q^2+1)^2}, y_{(2,1)} = \frac{q^2}{(q^2+1)^2} and y_{(1^3)} = 0. The sign block carries no weight: this is the trace radical of H_3(q) (Gram degeneracy) seen in one line.
  4. Number. Substituting q_0 gives 0.998562\ldots. This is the rational function through which the proton-to-electron ratio pins q_0 (which pin the numbers use).

The first three steps of the miniature are identities in \mathbb{Q}(q) and involve no measurement. The figure-eight word V^2 gives (h^4 + 3h^2 + 1)/(h^2+4) by the same route. Every value above is computed exactly by computations/intro/intro_worked_miniature_h3.py.

The order matters. The categorical steps fix shapes — which knots, which blocks, which weights — without reference to any measurement; the measured world enters only at step five, in the three numbers described next.
prose:intro-model-and-measurement:
Everything described so far is mathematics. The words electron, proton, mass and binding energy name constructions inside the model, and a statement about them is a statement about those constructions. The physical content of the paper is located in one place: where a quantity computed in the model is set beside a measured one — the CODATA fundamental constants, the Particle Data Group tables, the AME2020 atomic-mass evaluation. Those comparisons are the empirical claims, and the Physical Observations chapter collects them.

Three measured numbers are admitted, and only three. They are the calibration inputs, and they match one for one the three real degrees of freedom of the first cohomology of the genus-four state space (calibration–cohomology alignment; three calibration inputs):

  • the electron mass m_e fixes the unit of mass, the scale;
  • the neutron \beta-decay channel fixes the aether parameter q_0, the modulus. Its ideal proxy is the muon-to-electron mass ratio, through the figure-eight relation m_\mu/m_e = \mathrm{Vol}(4_1)/\hbar_q^2. Because the modulus is overdetermined, the computed values read its numerical value off the most precisely measured mass ratio available, m_{\mathfrak{p}}/m_e, and at that pin the muon ratio becomes a prediction (which pin the numbers use);
  • the pion channel fixes the one remaining orthogonal class, the meson scale.

Nothing else is fitted. In particular no object — a knot, a partition, a truncation order — is chosen because it reproduces a measured value; such a choice would be a fourth calibration in disguise (calibration discipline; epistemic status of the calibrations). Because m_e sets the unit by fiat, an absolute mass in MeV carries no information beyond the dimensionless ratio behind it, so the comparisons are made on ratios, binding energies, decay Q-values and mass splittings; the same boundary separates dimensionless \mathbb{Q}(q) clock grains and state-space moduli from empirical Compton and SI Planck length bridges (stratified spacetime, length, and distance scales).

The standard applied to each comparison is strict: a prediction is counted as meeting its target only when its residual is below one hundredth of the experimental uncertainty. The observations chapter reports every residual against that standard, including the misses, which at present are the majority. A derived quantity that misses is reported as a miss rather than tuned away, because only an untuned model can be corrected by what its errors teach.
prose:chapter-overview:
Part I: Foundations. This paper's destination is a concise table of dimensionless quantities set against measured constants—the muon-to-electron mass ratio, the kaon-to-pion mass ratio, the fine-structure constant—each computed from one algebraic skeleton and a single aether parameter. That skeleton is the subject of Part I.

Quantum Universes introduces the quantum universe (QU): the algebraic skeleton encoded in the rigid triple

  (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)

comprising a rigid monoidal category \mathbf{C}, a Frobenius–Hopf object A, and a fibre functor \tau. The Frobenius trace \int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1} acts as categorical integration, assigning a scalar to each algebra element. Coupled with Kähler differentials, it supplies the algebra with both integration and differentiation. The Frobenius self-duality A \cong A^{\vee} guarantees their compatibility: integrating then differentiating agrees with differentiating then integrating. Information is conserved. From this triple come the Frobenius relation, the dagger involution, and the Tannaka–Krein reconstruction of the symmetry group.

Quantum Observable Universes imposes exactly three cohomological constraints—observability, measurability, and volume—promoting the QU to a quantum observable universe (QOU). The volume axiom formalises size: the non-degenerate trace \int_A provides a volume form, so volume is not an external assumption. Self-duality within this constrained space forces the gauge group G = \mathrm{SU}_2(R), a coordinate q, and an ordering direction; the genus of the state space is then fixed at four by the Descartes condition rather than forced by self-duality. The QOU manifests as the archimedean tuple

  (\mathbf{C}, \varTheta, G, \mathcal{S}).

In this language, a Lagrangian forms a categorical trace. Every categorical action equals the trace of a single Lagrangian endomorphism \Phi \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A) dictating the dynamics:

  \mathfrak{S} = \mathrm{tr}(\Phi).

The dynamics enters through the categorical Dirac operator, blending the connection \nabla with its projection onto the internal time-flow (the Reeb derivation \xi):

  \mathcal{D}_\nabla = q^{-1}\nabla + (1 - q^{-1})\,\iota_\xi\nabla.

This reduces to the standard covariant derivative at q = 1. Coupling the Dirac operator to a state \psi \colon \mathbf{1} \to A gives the Lagrangian endomorphism of a QOU, the categorical Lagrangian

  \mathcal{L}_q(\nabla, \psi) = \mathcal{D}_\nabla^{2} + \psi^{\ast} \otimes \mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A),

where \psi^{\ast} = \int_A \circ S(\psi) is the adjoint section. It exists and is unique once \nabla, \psi, q and \xi are chosen. Its first summand is bosonic: the square \mathcal{D}_\nabla^{2} decomposes—forced by the Frobenius–Hopf structure—into two curvature terms, spatial curvature (Ricci) and internal gauge curvature (Yang–Mills). Its second summand, the coupling of the matter state \psi, supplies the third. The categorical action \mathfrak{S}_q = \mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{L}_q) sums these three components:

  \mathfrak{S}_q = \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl(q \cdot R_{\int}\bigr)}_{\text{gravity}} + \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl( F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla \bigr)}_{\text{gauge}} + \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl(\psi^{\ast} \otimes \mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi\bigr)}_{\text{matter}}.

Here R_{\int} denotes the Frobenius–Ricci endomorphism, F_\nabla denotes the connection curvature, and \psi^{\ast} is the Frobenius adjoint. Varying \mathfrak{S}_q recovers quantum analogues of the Einstein, Yang–Mills, and Dirac equations.

Models of QOUs examines concrete archimedean, p-adic, and finite-field realisations. The archimedean model maps directly to physical reality; non-archimedean models supply arithmetic analogues. This establishes the genus-four state space—Bring's surface.

Lifting and Descent resolves global extensions of local categorical data. The quantum lifting condition states that an object admits a lift if and only if its obstruction class \kappa(x) \in H^2(S, B) vanishes. The descent involution \hat{\tau} decomposes the algebra into observable (descended) and pre-observable (transient) modes. The lifting obstructions reduce to the genus of the base curve: \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}(M_0) = 2 - 2g with g \geq 1, and the Descartes condition fixes g = 4. The Kummer exact sequence filtrates the obstruction space, revealing an obstruction that vanishes at the levels n \mid \chi(A) and persists at every other level.

Part II: Structural Mechanics. Braids and Knots replaces continuum path integrals with discrete braid-group representations inside the Iwahori–Hecke algebra H_n(q). The aether parameter q fixes the crossing energy:

  E_\times = q + q^{-1} = [2]_q.

Specific braids and link closures map to particle identities: the unknot 0_1 models the neutrino, the three-strand braid \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 \in B_3 closing to the positive Hopf link T(2,2) models the electron (with the two-strand left trefoil T_{2,3} = 3_1 retained as the single-component alternative model), and higher (2,n) torus knots model the heavier leptons. The photon is a four-term Hecke element \gamma = \mathbf{1} + \varphi_0\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1}. Two-photon products generate the massive spectrum. In the topological volume model, the figure-eight knot volume enters the muon-to-electron mass ratio through

  \frac{\mathfrak{m}_\mu}{m_e} = \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(4_1)}{\hbar_q^{2}}, \qquad \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}.

The calibration has two layers. In the ideal calibration this relation is the CAL-2 proxy: it coordinatises the weak-sector aether modulus q_0, and inverting it gives q_0 \approx 1.10998. The computed values instead pin q_0 numerically on the proton-to-electron ratio m_{\mathfrak{p}}/m_e, which is measured far more precisely, so at that pin evaluating \mathrm{Vol}(4_1)/\hbar_{q_0}^{2} against the measured m_\mu/m_e is a model comparison. The two pins differ by about 11.6 ppb (which pin the numbers use).

Bring's Surface develops the geometry of the genus-four curve \Sigma_4 with \chi_{\mathrm{eu}} = -6, first Betti number b_1 = 8, hyperbolic Gauss–Bonnet area 12\pi under its (2,4,5) tiling, and maximal automorphism group S_5. Its colour tubes provide coordinates for spacetime and electromagnetic fields, while embeddable torus knots span the homology basis and saturate at genus four.

Knots, Particles, and Confinement establishes the knot–particle dictionary used throughout the monograph: pairwise braiding from the hexagon identities, quark and nucleon derivation from pair production, the hadron algebra and its knot factorisation, the Borromean baryon (6_3^2) whose stability is invariant under the three Reidemeister moves, the electroweak and Higgs sector as the even-twist torus-link triplet \{T(2,4), T(2,6), T(2,8)\} whose Seifert genera sum to 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 = -\chi(\Sigma_4), and the confinement hierarchy culminating in atomic and isotopic shells.

The Eightfold Way and Flavor Structure examines how these braid configurations assemble into meson and baryon multiplets. It separates two distinct objects that share the root type A_2: the Coxeter quotient W(A_2) \cong S_3 of three-strand braiding H_3(q), which holds unconditionally by construction, and the flavour Lie algebra \mathfrak{sl}_3, which enters through quantum Schur–Weyl duality only when the fibre dimension equals N = 3. The chapter derives the meson octet, the Borromean decuplet, the U-spin Coleman–Glashow and \Lambda–\Sigma^0 relations, and the octonionic stabilizer chain G_2 = \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{O}) \supset \mathrm{SU}(3)_{\mathrm{c}} that splits \mathrm{Im}(\mathbb{O}) \cong \mathbb{R}^7 into 1 \oplus 3 \oplus \bar{3}.

The Mass Endomorphism extracts mass from the spectral data of a single categorical endomorphism \mathcal{M}(K) \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(X_K). Mass is a categorical invariant given by the Jones–Markov trace \mathrm{tr}_M of the Hecke mass element \Phi_{\mathrm{mass}}(\beta) at the Markov parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1) (where the three-row weight y_{(1^3)} vanishes and is resolved by the Geer–Patureau-Mirand–Turaev modified trace), paired with the complex volume \mathfrak{V} that separates binding energy (\mathrm{Re}\,\mathfrak{V}) from the \beta-decay Q-value (\mathrm{Im}\,\mathfrak{V}).

q-Hyperbolic Geometry connects the algebraic trace to hyperbolic complement geometry and q-deformed kinematics. It constructs the categorical Möbius self-avoidance energy, the crossing-energy decomposition and skein bar-antisymmetry, Lagrange resolvents and q-momentum, knot-operator energy, and the spectral filter governing admissible braidings. For a knot K with complement volume \mathrm{Vol}(K) and per-block density \rho(K), the dimensionless mass ratio is the volume–density product:

The electron mass fixes the unit, so the formula is evaluated through dimensionless mass ratios and binding energies rather than absolute masses in MeV. Mass Analysis unites the geometric and Archimedean faces into a single computational pipeline. Every elementary-particle, gauge-boson, hadron, and nuclear mass ratio derives from three calibration inputs over \mathbb{Q}(q) without empirical curve-fitting.

prose:authors-note-compute:
The computations rest on a purpose-built stack. The core is a Rust library for Hecke algebras (Gröbner–Shirshov reduction to normal form, seminormal representations, Markov traces), with bindings to Python and WebAssembly. Semidefinite and linear programs are solved with a fork of the Clarabel interior-point solver extended to higher-precision arithmetic, so that the dual variables, which carry structural information here, are certified rather than read from double-precision output. Markov traces of long braid words are computed by peeling: the word is multiplied into the Hecke algebra one crossing at a time, reduced to Gröbner–Shirshov normal form after each step so the number of terms stays bounded, and the top generator is then removed with the Markov property, recursing down the tower H_n(q) \supset H_{n-1}(q) \supset \cdots \supset H_1(q), so no matrix representation of the algebra is ever built. The confinement structure of the bound states restricts the remaining work to the blocks it leaves active. The Markov property and normal-form reduction are standard, and these are engineering choices: no claim of novelty is made for them relative to the computer-algebra literature.

Expensive results are cached in the repository. Numerical witnesses are committed alongside the scripts that produce them, and prebuilt Lean libraries are kept on dedicated branches of the repository, so that the formalisation can be checked without rebuilding its dependencies from source.

sec:qou-intro:
A quantum universe is the purely categorical aether from which the framework later reads off physics: its axioms are chosen so that, once observability and a volume constraint are imposed, they force \mathrm{SU}_2(R) as the physical gauge group rather than assuming it. Before the axioms, it helps to have one instance in hand: \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), the category of representations of \mathrm{SU}(2), is a rigid braided monoidal category carrying a Frobenius--Hopf object, and it is the guiding example throughout this chapter. Its braiding is symmetric, which is the classical case; the one-parameter deformation that breaks the symmetry is extracted from the braiding in Chapter 2.

This chapter introduces the quantum universe (QU): a braided monoidal category equipped with a Frobenius--Hopf object, a fibre functor, and a differential calculus. Duals are not part of this definition. They are imposed in Chapter 2, on the quantum observable universe, where they carry the antiparticles; the constructions later in this chapter that do use duals — the involutive structure, the categorical Hodge star, the internal Poisson object — say so in their own hypotheses. The chapter opens with categorical preliminaries (§ Rigid monoidal categories), state the core axioms (§ The Quantum Universe), and derive their first consequences — the Frobenius relation, involutive structure, and Tannaka--Krein reconstruction (§ Consequences).

The QU axioms also support differential-geometric structures: categorical connections, jet objects, and the Hodge star (§ Structures). The passage from a quantum universe to a quantum observable universe — adding observability, measurability, and the volume constraint that forces \mathrm{SU}_2(R) as the gauge group — is the subject of Chapter 3.
sec:scheme-notation:
Notation: group schemes and projective spaces over R.

Every construction in this paper is formulated once over an arbitrary commutative ring R and specialises to any base — a reader working over \mathbb{Z}_p, \mathbb{F}_p, or \mathbb{C} reads the same axioms and the same proofs, only the ground ring changes. To keep that substitution visible, all algebraic groups and projective spaces are written with their base ring R explicit:

Object Notation Over \mathbb{C}
Special unitary group \mathrm{SU}_2(R) \mathrm{SU}(2)
Maximal torus / Reeb gauge group U_1(R) U(1)
Projective line \mathbb{P}^1(R) \mathbb{CP}^1 \cong S^2
Multiplicative group \mathbb{G}_m(R) = R^{\times} \mathbb{C}^{\times}

When the base ring is clear from context, \mathrm{SU}_2 abbreviates \mathrm{SU}_2(R) and \mathbb{P}^1 abbreviates \mathbb{P}^1(R). The category-theoretic definitions of this chapter and the next — the quantum universe and the quantum observable universe — are stated at this level of generality.
sec:rigid-monoidal-intro:
Why do the axioms of a physical theory land on a rigid braided monoidal category? Two lines of thought converge here. Composing physical processes in sequence and in parallel forces a monoidal structure. Superselection-sector analysis of local observables forces the same. Any compositional theory of physical systems settles into this framework, which is fixed here before stating the quantum-universe axioms.

This section defines the two structures separately, because the paper uses them at two different levels. A quantum universe is braided: it has interactions. A quantum observable universe is braided and rigid: it also has duals, hence antiparticles and closed knots.

Two examples stay in view: the polynomial ring \mathbb{C}[z] and the coordinate ring \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). Objects have tensor products and a unit over a base ring, making the category R-linear. In the rigid case every object V has a dual V^{\vee}, and the zig-zag (snake) equations make V^{\vee} a right dual. A braiding exchanges tensor factors. The symmetric case c_{Y,X} \circ c_{X,Y} = \mathrm{id} marks the classical limit.

The next section mounts the Frobenius--Hopf object, the fibre functor, and the differential calculus on this scaffold.
def:snake-identity:
Definition Snake identity. Let (\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1}) be a monoidal category. Let V be an object with dual V^{\vee}, evaluation \mathrm{ev} \colon V \otimes V^{\vee} \to \mathbf{1}, and coevaluation \mathrm{coev} \colon \mathbf{1} \to V^{\vee} \otimes V. The snake identities are the equations making (\mathrm{ev}, \mathrm{coev}) exhibit V^{\vee} as a right dual of V:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:snake-identities}
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=2.5em]
  V
    \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{coev}"]
    \ar[dr, "\mathrm{id}_V"']
  & V \otimes V^{\vee} \otimes V
    \ar[d, "\mathrm{ev} \otimes \mathrm{id}"]
  \\
  & V
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small (left snake identity)}
\end{gathered}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=2.5em]
  V^{\vee}
    \ar[r, "\mathrm{coev} \otimes \mathrm{id}"]
    \ar[dr, "\mathrm{id}_{V^{\vee}}"']
  & V^{\vee} \otimes V \otimes V^{\vee}
    \ar[d, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{ev}"]
  \\
  & V^{\vee}
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small (right snake identity)}
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}

The pair forms an exact pairing.
rem:snake-identity-remark: Remark The snake identities in the graphical calculus. In the graphical calculus, the composites in the snake identities trace an S-shaped curve that straightens to a vertical line.
def:rigid-monoidal-category:
Definition Rigid monoidal category. A monoidal category (\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1}) is a category equipped with a bifunctor \otimes \colon \mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{C}, a unit object \mathbf{1}, and natural isomorphisms expressing associativity and unitality:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:monoidal-axioms}
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em]
  (X \otimes Y) \otimes Z
    \ar[r, "\alpha_{X,Y,Z}", "\sim"']
  & X \otimes (Y \otimes Z)
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small (associativity)}
\end{gathered}
\qquad
\begin{gathered}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  \mathbf{1} \otimes X
    \ar[r, "\ell_X", "\sim"']
  & X
  & X \otimes \mathbf{1}
    \ar[l, "\rho_X"', "\sim"]
\end{tikzcd}
\\[-0.5em]
\text{\small (unitality)}
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}

The category is rigid if every object V has a dual V^{\vee} together with morphisms \mathrm{ev}_V \colon V \otimes V^{\vee} \to \mathbf{1} and \mathrm{coev}_V \colon \mathbf{1} \to V^{\vee} \otimes V satisfying the snake identities.

The category \mathbf{C} is R-linear for a commutative ring R without quasi-zeros if every hom-set is an R-module and composition is R-bilinear.

The category is braided monoidal if it has a natural isomorphism c_{X,Y} \colon X \otimes Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y \otimes X compatible with the associator and satisfying the hexagon axioms. The braiding is symmetric when c_{Y,X} \circ c_{X,Y} = \mathrm{id}. Given a braiding, the exterior power \Lambda^k V is the image of the antisymmetriser \mathrm{Alt}_k = \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\pi acting on V^{\otimes k}, where permutations act via c.
rem:monoidal-justification:
Remark Rationale for monoidal categories. Why is a rigid monoidal category the starting point for quantum-geometric structure? Two lines of reasoning converge.

Information-theoretic necessity. Picture two subsystems side by side. The tensor product \otimes joining them is the grammar of any physical system possessing inputs and outputs. A compositional language forces a monoidal category. Rigidity is the further demand that processes be reversible at the level of types: a system of type V bends around to become an input of type V^{\vee}, which is the content of the snake identities. That demand is separable from the first, and the paper keeps the two apart — a quantum universe is braided, a quantum observable universe is braided and rigid.

Physical reconstruction from superselection. Take an electric charge and its conjugate anticharge. Algebraic quantum field theory arrives at the same structure through superselection sectors. The category of superselection sectors is automatically rigid braided monoidal. The tensor product encodes charge composition. The braiding encodes exchange statistics. Rigidity encodes anticharges. Locality and covariance force the monoidal structure.
ex:rigid-monoidal-vect:
Example \mathbb{C}[z] and \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). Two rigid monoidal categories run through this paper: the degenerate baseline \mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}} and the classical example \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). Both arise as representations of a function algebra.

The polynomial ring \mathbb{C}[z] is the algebra of functions on \mathbb{C}. The category \mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}} of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces is the simplest \mathbb{C}-linear rigid monoidal category. The tensor product is V \otimes W, the unit is \mathbf{1} = \mathbb{C}, and the dual is V^{\vee} = \mathrm{Hom}(V, \mathbb{C}) with \mathrm{ev}(v \otimes f) = f(v).

The coordinate ring \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) is the algebra of polynomial functions on \mathrm{SU}(2), generated by matrix entries \alpha, \beta, \bar\alpha, \bar\beta with \alpha\bar\alpha + \beta\bar\beta = 1. The category \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) of finite-dimensional representations is \mathbb{C}-linear rigid monoidal. Its simple objects are the spin-j representations V_j (j = 0, \tfrac12, 1, \ldots). The fundamental object is V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2.
sec:quantum-universe-intro:
The monoidal scaffold acquires its universe structure through the compact group \mathrm{SU}(2). Its coordinate algebra \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) carries an integration and a left-invariant calculus. Abstracting from this, a quantum universe is a triple (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau): an R-linear braided monoidal category \mathbf{C}, a Frobenius--Hopf object A, and a fibre functor \tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}. The triple is non-empty, as \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) provides an instance. Duals are not required at this level; they arrive with the observable universe of Chapter 2.

The Frobenius data is geometric. On A, the calculus \Omega^1(A) is differentiation, and the Frobenius form \int_A is integration. Non-degeneracy of the pairing indicates a faithful measure. The Frobenius pairing is the composite \int_A \circ \mu \colon A \otimes A \to \mathbf{1}. Non-degeneracy ensures a coevaluation satisfying the snake identities. When A is simple, the axioms pin this composite down uniquely up to a scalar. On \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), the pairing recovers the L^2 inner product and Peter--Weyl orthogonality.

The fundamental object and higher-form complex follow. On \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), the left-invariant calculus is \Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}. The de Rham complex \Omega^k(A) = \bigwedge_A^k \Omega^1(A) follows, with d^2 = 0. The rank-2 generator V plays a central role under the fibre functor and Tannaka--Krein reconstruction. The simplicity of the unit object \mathbf{1} forces the uniqueness of the volume form.
def:quantum-universe:
Definition Quantum Universe. A quantum universe is a tuple (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) consisting of:

  1. an R-linear braided monoidal category \mathbf{C} over a commutative ring R, whose unit endomorphisms recover the ground ring: R \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}), r \mapsto r \cdot \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}},
  2. a distinguished object A \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathbf{C}) equipped with a Frobenius–Hopf algebra structure, spelled out in axiom 2,
  3. an R-linear faithful fibre functor \tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod},

satisfying the following four axioms:

  1. (Temporal braiding) The ordering \prec_c induced by the braiding c_{V,W} \colon V \otimes W \xrightarrow{\sim} W \otimes V on the basis of A indexed by braid words is well-founded.
  2. (Frobenius--Hopf) A carries compatible associative multiplication \mu, co-multiplication \Delta, unit \eta, co-unit \varepsilon, and antipode S. The space A acts on every V \in \mathbf{C} via a categorical representation \rho_V \colon A \otimes V \to V.
  3. (Symmetric Frobenius) The left and right categorical traces on \mathrm{End}(A) coincide. These traces are defined by the self-duality of A, which the snake identities for the pairing \int_A \circ\, \mu supply in axiom 2. (This equality specifies the untwisted \nu = \mathrm{id}_A specialization, realized on \mathcal{O}(G) at the symmetric point and on weight-centralizer endomorphism algebras; when the Haar state on a quantised coordinate ring carries a non-trivial modular Nakayama automorphism \nu, one has \mathrm{tr}_L(f) = \mathrm{tr}_R(f \circ \nu) on \mathrm{End}(A), while categorical traces on representations remain untwisted via the balancing twist.)
  4. (Wedderburn semisimplicity) A is semisimple, with a finite index set \widehat{A} of blocks. Each block \lambda \in \widehat{A} carries a central idempotent p_\lambda, and these
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{do not mix:} && p_\lambda \circ p_\mu &= 0 && (\lambda \neq \mu), \\
\text{and span:}   && \textstyle\sum_{\lambda \in \widehat{A}} p_\lambda &= \mathrm{id}_A. &&
\end{aligned}
\]

Each block further carries a Frobenius weight \int_A p_\lambda invertible in R, and a quantum dimension \dim_q(\lambda) invertible in R.

Rigidity of \mathbf{C} is not required here. It is imposed one level up, on a quantum observable universe (Chapter 2), where duals carry the antiparticles.

On the ground ring. R is a commutative ring, not a field, and "invertible in R" in axiom 4 is strictly stronger than "nonzero" once R has non-units. The two clauses coincide only over a field.

On the aether parameter. The axioms ask of R only that it be a commutative ring. No deformation parameter appears among the data: the balancing twist supplied by the tensor product and the braiding determines one on the defining representation, it lands in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R, and Chapter 2 reads it off there. The invertibility in axiom 4 is quantified over this universe's own blocks, so it constrains the pair (R, \mathbf{C}) and not R alone. A ring therefore limits which decompositions it can carry rather than being admissible or not. Which rings carry the non-degenerate decompositions the later chapters use is settled in Chapter 2, once the parameter is available, and the answer is a property of a construction of a quantum universe, not an extra axiom of the definition.

The identification R \cong \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}) in item 1 is a genuine hypothesis and not a consequence of R-linearity. Linearity supplies only the ring map r \mapsto r \cdot \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}; its bijectivity is the statement that \mathbf{1} is simple, and it is what licenses reading the block data \int_A p_\lambda and \dim_q(\lambda) as elements of R rather than as endomorphisms of the unit. It is stated here because the rest of the paper uses it silently — for instance in reading the aether parameter as an element of \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}).
rem:quantum-universe-axiom-motivation:
Remark What each axiom buys. Each item of the definition answers a physical question. This remark says which; the precise consequences are proved later.

Why braided. Two systems sitting side by side can be exchanged, and in three dimensions the exchange is a process, not a relabelling: passing V in front of W is a different operation from passing it behind. A symmetric braiding forgets the difference, and that is the classical limit — ordinary bosons and fermions, where a swap is undone by a swap. Keeping the difference is what lets a strand hold a knot, and what lets an exchange accumulate a phase.

The hexagon identities carried by the braiding buy something further, and it is the reason "an interaction" is a well-defined notion at all. Within one interaction the pairwise exchanges may be performed in more than one order, and the hexagons say the orders agree: braiding a composite system past a third is the same as braiding its parts past it one at a time, and the two ways of resolving a triple crossing give the same operator. So an interaction is determined by which strands cross, not by the order in which the crossings happen to be written down. Chapter 9 makes this precise and draws the consequence: every many-body interaction is a word in two-strand crossings, which is why the particle dictionary is built from pairwise data.

Why the well-founded ordering (axiom 1). Exchange has a direction, and the ordering \prec_c it induces admits no infinite descending chain. Every process therefore terminates in a normal form. This is the sense in which time is an ordering here rather than a coordinate: what makes a "before" is that the reduction stops.

Why Frobenius–Hopf (axiom 2). The object A is the algebra of the universe's internal symmetry operations. Multiplication composes two of them, the antipode inverts one, the unit is doing nothing, and the Frobenius form averages over all of them. The action \rho_V says every object of the universe carries a representation of A.

The classical picture is \mathrm{SO}(3). Rotations compose, every rotation has an inverse, and one can average a quantity over all of them; every physical body carries a representation, so no observable depends on which frame was chosen to describe it. Axiom 2 asserts exactly that invariance for an aether whose rotation group is deformed. Where \mathrm{SO}(3) gives rotational invariance, A gives invariance of the observables under the aether's own symmetry, and the deformation is what distinguishes the two.

Why symmetric Frobenius (axiom 3). A closed loop must have one amplitude. Closing a worldline on the left and closing it on the right are two ways of computing the same number, and axiom 3 requires them to agree. Without it "the trace of a process" is ambiguous, and mass — which is read off a trace — would depend on a drawing convention.

Why semisimplicity (axiom 4). The aether must have channels. Semisimplicity is the statement that any state of A resolves into elementary pieces which do not mix, and that there are finitely many kinds of them. The two halves are separate demands and the axiom makes both explicit: the idempotents are pairwise orthogonal, so a state resolving into one channel has no component in another; and they sum to the identity, so the channels exhaust A and nothing is left unaccounted for. Without the first there is no clean spectrum, without the second there are states admitting no decomposition into elementary ones, and either way there is no particle spectrum to speak of.

The two invertibility conditions say that no channel is degenerate: a block whose Frobenius weight is not invertible would be present in the algebra yet carry no usable share of any trace, and a block whose quantum dimension is not invertible could not be normalised against. Over a field this is just non-vanishing; over a ring it is the stronger demand, and it is the stronger one that is meant.

Once the blocks exist and are non-degenerate, the co-Casimir trace

  \mathrm{tr}_M(C_{\dim_q}) \;=\; \sum_{\lambda \in \widehat{A}} \frac{1}{\dim_q(\lambda)}

follows by linearity of the trace over the central idempotents. It is a consequence of the axioms, proved in the mass-theory chapter, and is not assumed here. The total trace distributes over the channels, each contributing in inverse proportion to its quantum dimension — wide channels cheap, narrow ones expensive. That is the bookkeeping which later lets a mass be attached to a knot rather than to a diagram of one.

What is deliberately absent. Rigidity. A quantum universe need not have duals. Duals are what allow a strand to bend backwards, which is what an antiparticle is and what closing a knot requires, and they are imposed one level up, on a quantum observable universe.
prop:quantum-universe-exists: Proposition Existence of quantum universes. The four quantum universe axioms are jointly satisfiable. There exists a triple (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) satisfying them.
prf:quantum-universe-exists: Proof Proof of existence of quantum universes. Witness: \mathbf{C} = R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod} (finite-dimensional R-modules) with A = R as the trivial Frobenius--Hopf algebra, \tau = \mathrm{id}, and \Omega^1(R) = 0. Since \Omega^1(R) = 0 the differential-calculus axiom holds vacuously, and A = R carries the ground-ring Frobenius--Hopf structure, so each remaining axiom is satisfied trivially. A richer witness is \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) with A the regular representation, worked out in the next section. Both establish existence.
sec:tau-notation:
Notation: the forgetful functor \tau.

The forgetful functor is denoted \tau to avoid conflict with differential-form notation (\omega_i, \omega_V). The choice of \tau carries physical and mathematical resonances:

  • Tannakian reconstruction. The letter \tau recalls the Tannaka--Krein theorem reconstructing the gauge group G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau).
  • Trace / integration. In von Neumann algebras, a faithful normal state is denoted \tau. The forgetful functor underlies the Frobenius integration \int_A, whose notation is fixed in Chapter 2.
  • Proper time. In the archimedean realisation, \tau represents the observer's proper time. It parameterises the emergence of R-modules from the abstract category.
def:frobenius-pairing:
Definition Frobenius pairing. The Frobenius pairing makes A self-dual. The motivating instance is the Haar pairing on the coordinate ring of \mathrm{SU}(2) (see example).

Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe with multiplication \mu \colon A \otimes A \to A and Frobenius form \int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}. The Frobenius pairing is the composite:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:frobenius-pairing}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  A \otimes A \ar[r, "\mu"]
  & A \ar[r, "\int_A"]
  & \mathbf{1}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

The Frobenius pairing is non-degenerate when it induces an isomorphism A \xrightarrow{ \sim } A^{\vee}. Equivalently, the snake identities hold: there exists a coevaluation \tilde{\eta} \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A such that the composites

A \xrightarrow{\rho^{-1}} A \otimes \mathbf{1}
  \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id} \otimes \tilde{\eta}} A \otimes A \otimes A
  \xrightarrow{\alpha^{-1}} (A \otimes A) \otimes A
  \xrightarrow{(\int_A \circ \mu) \otimes \mathrm{id}} \mathbf{1} \otimes A
  \xrightarrow{\lambda_A} A

and its mirror equal \mathrm{id}_A. For \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) and A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) it is the L^2 pairing of the Haar integral, under which the matrix coefficients of the spin-j representation pair with weight 1/(2j+1), the inverse of its dimension.
prop:frobenius-pairing-exists:
Proposition Existence of the Frobenius pairing. The Frobenius form makes the multiplication a non-degenerate pairing, yielding the self-duality A \cong A^\vee. It sends a pair (a, b) to the scalar \int_A(\mu(a, b)).

Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe with multiplication \mu and Frobenius form \int_A. The non-degenerate Frobenius pairing \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle = \int_A \circ \mu exists as a morphism in \mathbf{C}. Its adjoint A \to A^\vee is an isomorphism. Uniqueness up to scalar is the subject of the next section.
prf:frobenius-pairing-exists:
Proof Proof of existence of the Frobenius pairing. The pairing in question is attached to the Frobenius object A: its value is the composite \int_A \circ \mu, and its non-degeneracy is the invertibility of the induced adjoint A \to A^\vee.

Existence is immediate: \mu and \int_A are part of the quantum- universe data, so the composite \int_A \circ \mu is a morphism in \mathbf{C} by composition.

Non-degeneracy is where the provenance matters. A quantum universe is not rigid — \mathbf{C} carries no duality functor, so there is no ambient A^\vee to map into and no ambient snake identities to invoke. What plays that role is supplied by axiom 2 on A alone: the Frobenius–Hopf structure carries a coevaluation \tilde\eta \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A together with the two snake identities for the pairing \mathrm{ev} = \int_A \circ\, \mu. Those identities exhibit A as its own dual; they are not consequences of a rigid structure on \mathbf{C}, and asserting them is exactly what axiom 2 does.

The pairing is therefore non-degenerate because the Frobenius–Hopf data says so, and the self-duality A \cong A^\vee is a conclusion about A rather than an instance of a duality every object enjoys. Rigidity is imposed one level up, on a quantum observable universe (Chapter 2).
sec:quantum-universe-frobenius-pairing-u:
Pinning the Frobenius pairing on the fundamental object A makes the \mathrm{SU}(2) realisation canonical. The pairing is unique, forcing its explicit \mathrm{SU}(2) form. Every downstream construction inherits this fixed choice.

This sub-section proves the pairing unique and exhibits the \mathrm{SU}(2) realisation. The arc proceeds through:

  1. The uniqueness proof for the pairing on A.
  2. The explicit \mathrm{SU}(2) pairing realisation.
  3. The geometric role of the pairing in the aether-flow.
  4. The canonical \mathrm{SU}(2) explication and table data.
  5. The higher-forms identification.
prop:frobenius-pairing-unique:
Proposition Uniqueness of the Frobenius pairing. The Frobenius pairing is canonical up to overall scale. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe with A simple. Any two non-degenerate Frobenius forms \int_A^{(1)}, \int_A^{(2)} differ by an invertible scalar:

  \int_A^{(2)} \;=\; c  \int_A^{(1)}
  \qquad\text{for some } c \in \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}).

The induced Frobenius pairings \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_i = \int_A^{(i)} \circ \mu differ by the same scalar.
prf:frobenius-pairing-unique: Proof Proof of uniqueness of the Frobenius pairing. Uniqueness reduces to the one-dimensionality of the relevant Hom-space: when A is simple, a Schur-type argument forces a one-dimensional space of forms, so any two Frobenius forms must agree up to a unit scalar. Concretely, each non-degenerate \int_A^{(i)} \colon A \to \mathbf{1} factors uniquely through the isomorphism A \xrightarrow{\sim} A^\vee as a morphism A^\vee \to \mathbf{1}. The space \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(A^\vee, \mathbf{1}) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, A) \otimes \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, A^\vee) is one-dimensional when A is simple, by the Schur-type argument above. Hence any two Frobenius forms differ by a unit scalar c, and the composite \int_A^{(2)} \circ \mu = c \cdot \int_A^{(1)} \circ \mu inherits the same scaling.
ex:frobenius-pairing-su2:
Example The Frobenius pairing on \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). The Frobenius pairing is made concrete on \mathrm{SU}(2), with the coordinate ring and Haar integral of the \mathrm{SU}(2) example below.

Set A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) with pointwise multiplication \mu(f \otimes g) = fg and Haar integral \int_A f = \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f(x)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(x). The bilinear Frobenius pairing is

  \langle f, g \rangle_A
  =  \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f(x)g(x)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(x),

which relates to the sesquilinear L^2 / GNS inner product via complex conjugation: \langle f, g \rangle_{L^2} = \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} \overline{f(x)}g(x)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(x) = \langle \bar{f}, g \rangle_A.

Non-degeneracy. Haar measure has full support: for any f \in A, setting \phi = \bar{f} \in A gives \langle \phi, f \rangle_A = \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} |f(x)|^2\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(x), so \langle \phi, f \rangle_A = 0 for all \phi \in A forces f = 0. The Peter--Weyl theorem provides an orthogonal basis of matrix coefficients \{D^j_{mn}\} satisfying

  \langle \overline{D^j_{mn}}, D^{j'}_{m'n'} \rangle_A
  =  \frac{1}{2j+1}\delta_{jj'}\delta_{mm'}\delta_{nn'}.

(On the non-symmetric quantum deformation of \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) constructed in the next chapter, Woronowicz's Peter--Weyl orthogonality replaces 2j + 1 by the categorical dimension \dim_q(V_j) and weights each row index m by the modular Nakayama factor of the Haar state.) The isomorphism A \xrightarrow{\sim} A^{\vee} sends \overline{D^j_{mn}} to the dual coordinate functional of D^j_{mn} scaled by 1/(2j+1).

Concrete calculation on \mathbb{C}^2. The matrix generators of \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) are \alpha, \beta, \bar{\alpha}, \bar{\beta} with |\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1. The spin-\tfrac{1}{2} coefficients are D^{1/2}_{mn} \in \{\alpha, \beta, -\bar{\beta}, \bar{\alpha}\}, and the bilinear pairing evaluates to

  \langle \bar{\alpha}, \alpha \rangle_A = \tfrac{1}{2}, \qquad \langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle_A = 0, \qquad \langle \bar{\alpha}, \beta \rangle_A = 0.

The factor \tfrac{1}{2} confirms the normalisation for spin j = \tfrac{1}{2}.

The snake identity. The coevaluation \tilde{\eta} \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A sends 1 \mapsto \sum_{j,m,n} (2j+1)D^j_{mn} \otimes \overline{D^j_{mn}}. The composite A \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id} \otimes \tilde{\eta}} A \otimes A \otimes A \xrightarrow{(\int_A \circ \mu) \otimes \mathrm{id}} A acts as:

  f  \longmapsto  \sum_{j,m,n} (2j+1)
  \langle f, D^j_{mn} \rangle_A \cdot \overline{D^j_{mn}} = f.

This is \mathrm{id}_A, confirming non-degeneracy.
rem:frobenius-geometric-role:
Remark Frobenius structure as categorical integration. The Frobenius structure on A provides integration in the categorical calculus. The quantum universe pairs:

  • Differentiation: the Kähler differentials \Omega^1(A) measure infinitesimal change within A.
  • Integration: the Frobenius form \int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1} assigns a scalar to each element of A.

Non-degeneracy of the Frobenius pairing means the measure is faithful: \int_A ab = 0 for all b implies a = 0. Differentiation and integration are therefore both internal to A.
ex:quantum-universe-su2:
Example \mathrm{SU}(2) as a quantum universe. Continuing rigid monoidal Vect, the quantum universe axioms are checked here for G = \mathrm{SU}(2).

(i) Category. \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) is the category of finite-dimensional complex representations. This is a \mathbb{C}-linear rigid monoidal category. The G-action on tensor products is diagonal; on duals it is the contragredient.

(ii) Frobenius--Hopf object. A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) is the coordinate ring. Its Hopf structure encodes the group operations (see Table 1). The Frobenius pairing is positive definite.

(iii) Fibre functor. \tau \colon \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) \to \mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}} is the forgetful functor. It is exact, faithful, and monoidal. By Tannaka--Krein duality, G \cong \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau).

(iv) Differential calculus. The left-invariant calculus on \mathrm{SU}(2) provides \Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}. The universal derivation d \colon A \to \Omega^1(A) acts by df = \sum_i (\partial_i f) \omega_i.

(v) Braiding. In \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) the braiding is the flip c_{V,W}(v \otimes w) = w \otimes v, which is symmetric: c_{W,V} \circ c_{V,W} = \mathrm{id}. The first axiom asks for the ordering \prec_c that a braiding induces on the basis indexed by braid words. That ordering is well-founded for any braiding, the flip included, as the statement on braiding-induced orderings in the next chapter makes precise; non-symmetry c_{V,V}^{2} \neq \mathrm{id} is not used on words. So the example verifies all four axioms. What the flip lacks is non-symmetry on states: each crossing has order two, so exchange on states closes into chains. The example is the symmetric point of a one-parameter family whose braiding is not symmetric: the representation categories of the quantum deformation of \mathrm{SU}(2), constructed in the next chapter. On V \otimes V the braiding of a member of that family acts on the symmetric and antisymmetric parts by two scalars with product -1 whose ratio is not -1, so it satisfies a quadratic relation with two distinct roots and is not symmetric [kassel1995]. Items (i)--(iv) deform to the family with the same simple objects and the same Clebsch--Gordan rule, the Haar state h_A in place of the Haar measure, and the three-dimensional left-covariant calculus in place of the left-invariant forms; what changes away from the symmetric point is both the braiding, which for a generic member of the family has infinite order on states, and the trace symmetry on the quantised coordinate ring, where h_A ceases to vanish on commutators and becomes twisted by Woronowicz's modular Nakayama automorphism \nu (h_A(ab) = h_A(b\,\nu(a))) while untwisted trace symmetry persists on the Cartan weight centralizer and on ribbon traces of representations. In a suitable normalisation the deformed braiding is the flip plus a diagonal correction that vanishes at the symmetric point, which is the sense in which the symmetric example is the limit of the braided ones.

def:higher-forms:
Definition Higher differential forms. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe with differential calculus \Omega^1(A). The higher differential forms are the graded A-bimodule:

  \Omega^k(A) =  \bigwedge\nolimits_A^k \Omega^1(A), \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots

Here \Omega^0(A) = A. For an object V, \Lambda^k V denotes its k-th exterior power. The differential d \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A) extends the universal derivation by the graded Leibniz rule and satisfies d^2 = 0:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:de-rham-complex}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  A = \Omega^0(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \Omega^2(A) \ar[r, "d"]
  & \cdots
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad (d^2 = 0)
\end{equation}
ex:higher-forms-su2:
Example Higher forms on \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)). On A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), the left-invariant calculus has \Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}. The group is three-dimensional, so the exterior tower truncates at k = 3:

  • \Omega^0(A) = A
  • \Omega^1(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}
  • \Omega^2(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2, \omega_1 \wedge \omega_3, \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\}
  • \Omega^3(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\}
  • \Omega^k(A) = 0 for k \geq 4.

The differential d is determined by d\omega_i = -\tfrac{1}{2} \epsilon_{ijk}\omega_j \wedge \omega_k.
